I cautiously recommend this game. It's great on the whole, but there were a couple design choices which [b]really[/b] bugged me and nearly caused me to give a thumbs down. Those two things were: [b]the usage of RNG & the game's subsequent reliance on rollbacks (do-overs).[/b]

I'm a huge fan of hacking games. They are one of my favorite niche-genres of games. Generally speaking, the gameplay in a hacking game follows a simple formula: poke at a "server" and strip its defenses using various tools until it can be "connected to." This is often done with a time limit.

Midnight Protocol challenges this formula by translating the process into a turn based affair. In many ways, it plays like a turn based RPG. On a conceptual level, this is a cool idea. I was excited when I read about it. In practice, however, I found that it [strike]encouraged[/strike] [b]mandated[/b] save scumming. I mean this as constructively as possible - [b]I hate this.[/b]

I'll elaborate:

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b], it was because I wasn't fast enough. The onus was on [b]ME[/b] to improve my skills. I needed to be faster. I had all the tools, but I came up short.

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Midnight Protocol[/i][/b], it was because [b]the game's RNG[/b] dealt me an [i]objectively unwinnable[/i] scenario. The SysOp wandered into my node, or the "random" trace mechanic in Pavo's mission installed a Sundrop 10 nodes away.

This isn't interesting or engaging gameplay. I'm not learning anything, and I'm not becoming a better player. I'm just waiting for a luckier break.

Now, it would be one thing if you could "embrace failure" like you can in a game like XCOM or Rimworld - but you can't in Midnight Protocol. Most key missions actually prevent you from disconnecting until you complete your main objective. You are expected to rollback if you fail.

[i]My next two particular criticisms were addressed in a patch on 10/18/21. Respect.[/i]

[strike]RNG isn't the only thing causing me to rollback missions. The game gives you a peek at what kind of nodes & defenses you will be up against, allowing you to choose the appropriate programs for the job. For rank & file side-missions, this generally isn't a big deal. But for some of the larger story missions, you need fairly specific loadouts to have a fighting chance. It's not uncommon for me to get 8+ turns into a mission before I find myself thinking "Yeah I can't do this without Tunnel" and rolling back.

But it gets a little worse - ICE can be hidden... [i]and its location in missions is static.[/i] This means that after I (am forced to) rollback, I now know where the ICE is, and the mission is partially spoiled. It's up to me if I want to "pretend" not to know that.[/strike]

I've spent a lot of real estate here ragging on the RNG/Rollback mechanics, but I want to reiterate that I still recommend this game.

When the RNG gods [i]aren't[/i] busy strangling me, I actually really enjoy the turn based gameplay. It's a welcome twist on the genre that makes it feel truly different. The presentation is phenomenal (would have liked some more lively music though). And I really like the open ended narrative allowing you to chase leads & reply to emails. Simulation is an important part of hacking games, and I love the agency that the game gives us.

Well polished hacking games are an extreme rarity. There's been like... 5 since Uplink came out in 2001. I'm happy this game exists and I'm enjoying my time with it on the whole. I just wish RNG wasn't so strongly relied upon in its design.

[b]My Playtime:[/b] 29h (100% achievement, finished the game)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (~9 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] is a simple turn-based strategy game with a hacking theme. You'll be able to explore nodes in a network and use programs to get data from them. The game offers multiple story branching, missions, and unlockables based on the path that you choose.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- Story branching depends on your choice in the mission
- 2 endings
- Those who don't like to read can still enjoy the game without doing so
- Various programs and hardware to use based on the mission and playstyle
- Difficulty can be changed anytime you want

[b]Cons:[/b]
- RNG-based, especially at the beginning of the game
- It can take a while to wait until the enemy finishes their turn
- Missions will be treated as finished if you exit the network
- Contrasting colors in some cutscenes (red on top of black/grey) can be problematic to some people

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you enjoy playing hacking games and don't mind playing one in a different genre, buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The visuals are divided into two parts: your computer and the network interface. The computer interface is more simplified, giving a lot of space to the text with switchable tabs. As for the network, they are depicted with a lot of interconnected nodes that you can travel to. To be honest, they don't look like a network at all, but the programs' visuals help to give that impression.

[h3]Story[/h3]
Dialogues in [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] are mostly about missions that you will take. A lot of events will happen at the same time as the main plot, which will get you involved in various things. I liked that they usually don't stop after one mission - it feels as if I was involved and making progress. As for the main plot, I found them to be alright. The presentation looks cool with the sudden contract of color, although some parts are still in mystery. The closure also feels realistic with everything going by as normal. However, despite the multiple endings, I don't think they differ that much to warrant another playthrough.

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
As I said before, the game is a turn-based strategy, albeit simplified. You'll have a series of interconnected nodes where you can travel and spawn programs to help you with your objectives. The objectives are varied in each mission, but basically, you need to explore all nodes and take out every object of interest, whether it's by downloading a file or routing money to your account. Some ICEs will guard some nodes in between, forcing you to spawn another program to take them out. Moreover, you need to do these while avoiding being traced, which will be randomized per turn based on your stealth capabilities.

Stealth is the most problematic aspect of this game. You only have a 75% chance not to be recognized enemy for each turn, and that's by using all of your slices, which is the equivalent of your system memory in-game. However, you will eventually need to summon more programs to do other things, which will require more slices. You can always lower the assigned slices in your stealth program, but doing so will lower its capabilities, making it easier for you to be traced by the enemy. I had to restart a mission several times in the beginning whenever the RNG screw me up and traced me every turn. It was boring to replay the missions and do the same thing again, hoping that the outcome will be different. The gear upgrades that were given after you play some missions help to overcome this, but you still need to tough it out before you got to that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759479057

The early game is tough. Not only is the stealth mechanic isn't reliable, but the randomized enemies also can screw your run. You need to walk efficiently and not waste turns due to the RNG-based stealth, but enemies' locations are always hidden until you ran into them or used a sniffer program. Both options are not good either - the first option will increase your trace bar while the second one will eat 2 slices for 2 turns. It is easier to memorize enemies' locations before attempting your real run, but some enemies are placed randomly between more than one path. Again, this can be mitigated by purchasing upgrades after you reach a certain point.

The game gets better after you get enough upgrades. The RNG-based gameplay is still there, but it won't affect much to your experience. Moreover, numerous programs are available to help you build a deck that suits your playstyle. Since some missions are easier if you bring a certain program, you're bound to swap the programs from time to time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2632524112

The reputation system can increase your difficulty. The game has a system that categorizes you into either white hat, grey hat, or black hat. This gives an impression that you can only choose one, although you can get as many reputations as you want in all categories. Some story-related missions might give a different reputation and outcome based on your action, but you never have to worry about anything apart from that. I refrained from taking anything that might increase my black hat reputation at first, which only penalize me from getting a benefit from that category and more money.

Money is limited at the early game. This might give issues to those who are trying to play the game purely as white hats since they are restricted from taking money from certain nodes. Moreover, those who quit the mission halfway will get penalized even more since the mission will be treated as completed without getting any reward. The game will give you a lot of money near the end of the game, but you won't need it at that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759480074

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
The in-game clock says that I finished the game at 15:50:34, although [i]Steam[/i] said that I finished it in 26.6h. I had to retry some levels a few times to get a perfect result, and since you need to go to the main menu to buy more gears at the store in missions, it can take a while to load your save, especially with the unskippable animations. I spent the rest of my playtime figuring out the last achievement, which can be made shorter if you know what to do.

As for the difficulty, it can be hard at the beginning due to the RNG, but you can always change the difficulty in the options. I didn't change it apart from one mission, which I deemed impossible to finish at the normal difficulty due to the time limit. The final boss might also pose a problem if you choose to go on a certain route, although it is still doable by using certain programs.

[b]Problems[/b]
Some text can be hard to see due to the font color. Also, the in-game display can hinder you from seeing some information, such as the node address and how many turns you have left.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] might be unpleasant to play at first due to the RNG, but it will soon be enjoyable once you have access to certain upgrades. My focus went to completing missions instead of the story, which is always unique in certain aspects. The game also offers more gameplay through the Workshop feature, although I soon got bored since I had to deal with the RNG again without my upgrades. Although I found some aspects to be lacking, I still could recommend [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] at a sale, provided that you are fine with the RNG-based gameplay.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Midnight Protocol[/h1]

Interesting game, a wonderful time killer and definitely a hidden gem. I really wonder why more people aren't playing it. The game mixes hacking, puzzles, and storytelling into one fun little experience. It's nothing new, the story is just above average and there are a few flaws. And if you've played games like Uplink, Hacknet, Nite Team 4, or even the hacking part of the new Shadowrun games, you'll be familiar with most parts of the gameplay. But overall I have no hesitation in recommending the game at full price and definitely on sale.

[b]Postive:[/b]

1.) Immersion and atmosphere are top notch. The beginning is a bit rough, boring and repetitive, but it picks up the pace pretty quickly and doesn't slow down until the end. After the tutorial and the first few standard missions you can't and don't want to stop. Just "one" more mission and hours later, after some really intense battles and boss fights, you start to see the full potential of the game.

2.) Some missions and side missions are the real deal. I've had some of the most intense moments in recent memory, taking on other hackers or "bosses" in some highly dynamic puzzle battles. And not even in real time, just by typing commands into my keyboard. This is a great achievement by the developers. And some of the side missions are really well written.

3.) The soundtrack is great and a wonderful addition to the immersion and intensity during most missions.

4.) Graphics and user interface are minimalistic but quite polished. There is nothing to complain about.  didn't notice any bugs or crashes either.

[b]Neutral:[/b]

1.) The story could be a lot better. It's your well-known sci-fi/cyper story that you've heard, read, or seen many times. Maybe it would be ok if it was your first cyber/hacking game, but a little creativity here and the game would be a real masterpiece.

2.) The gameplay is strange at first. There doesn't seem to be much depth. But once you get used to the keyboard-only mechanics and get more and more programs and hardware to work with, the possibilities and depth get pretty good. You can build your deck based on your playstyle, but there are always some limitations on what programs you should bring. And some are just better than others. It's still good, but that's definitely a point where the game could be better. And that RNG can really mess thing up. 

[b]Cons:[/b]

1.) There is no manual saving. Yes, I understand it. It "adds" to the immersion or something like that. But in a game where you can take different paths and make certain decisions, I think a save function is an absolute must. Even more so when you have to play and answer certain side missions perfectly in order to see everything the game has to offer. And it's not so clear what to answer or what to do to advance the side story and get the next mission. I got pretty pissed when I read about things I missed while being very careful to avoid doing just that. But one wrong answer, or move and that's it. Better luck next time. I don't like this decision at all.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

I don't know the full story behind the game and the devs, but only 131 reviews for a great title like this is just sad. It's about 25-30 hours of gameplay, fun, and intensity. It's a solid piece of work with a lot of commitment put into it and well worth the price and I hope more people find out about this hidden gem. If you like hacking/puzzle games or want to get into it, don't be shy. Try it out and if you like it, spread the word. Midnight Protocol deserves a good community as so far there are no achievement guides, walktroughts or tips for specific missions, deck/hardware discussions and the like.

review_text_raw:
This game is currently in the Humble Choice for January 2022.   If you are interested in the game and it's before February 1st, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

A keyboard-based hacking game.

Midnight Protocol calls itself a tactical RPG, though I disagree. Midnight Protocol is a strange keyboard-based game that completely removes the mouse from the game. It also is a hacking simulator where players have to breach networks that are more similar to Uplink or Hacknet. Though controlling the entire experience through just a command line makes for a very interesting experience. 

I’m a little shocked to announce this isn’t made by Zachtronics, and yet still really feels like a Zachtronics style game. The entire game gives the player the power to breach networks and then adds moral choices such as robbing random people and earning profits as a black hat hacker, or trying to remain noble as a white hat hacker. There’s a strong narrative as well, which is intriguing. 

Pick this up if you think you’d be willing to play a keyboard-based command-line game. The game is interesting and unique as you’ll see but if you aren’t intrigued by a game that only allows the player to use the keyboards, this one probably won’t be for you. It’s a special game, yet I adore this one. 

If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel: https://youtu.be/j3gs3-4WiQI

review_text_raw:
This is a game that while via screenshots, doesn't look like much, is a very very cool unique take on the "hacking" genre.  It's entirely keyboard driven, and while that may feel like a hindrance, it actually adds to the game's immersion.  All controls are well thought out and seamless, and there's no awkward switching between mouse and keyboard like many typical games might do.

The gameplay itself is a little bit puzzle and a healthy dose of turn based tactics.  There's some RNG involved, and while you can't save scum individual moves, restarting a level is quick and painless, so if you really get boned by RNG (rare but could happen), you don't feel bad giving it another shot.

Honestly, it feels like XCOM in how it feels to do well (or poorly), getting a few lucky dice rolls, or missing a few 90% shots, but there's usually enough wiggle room baked in that it doesn't ruin your run.

There's also a cool RPG-ish element of progression.  As you get further, you buy new programs and hardware to customize your abilities.  Do you want to be stealthy and slow?  Do you want to be fast and brash?  Do you need a sniper program to deal with a long range enemy, or one that helps you open additional paths from a distance to skirt a danger?

On top of all that, the presentation is much slicker in game than screenshots may reveal.  Everything is cohesive in feel, animated in a flashy, but appropriate manner.  The sound effects and music are very hacker feeling and enjoyable. 

Finally, there's actually a story!  I'm still going through it, so I can't comment on its entire arc, but it involves you working with friends to accomplish various goals, and there's a range of personal crisis, professional concerns, morality.  It actually feels somewhat real, like you're actually emailing other people, and it adds some reasons to what you're doing.

All in all, an unusual game that's well worth playing.

I received this game via a Humble Choice pack, and I have very mixed feelings. There are times like this when I wish that Steam had something more complicated than a binary review system.  This game is fun, and I enjoy the mechanics and plot greatly, BUT.  And this is a VERY IMPORTANT BUT.

The game requires a lot of patience to play and enjoy.  This is not just because of the mechanics itself, which can be convoluted and easy to accidentally mess up, the most important of which is that you can only bring so many programs with you onto a mission, and sometimes you don't realize you've brought the wrong ones until it's too late and you have to start over with a new set up (which brings us to another issue, your inability to leave a mission early without irrevocably failing it.  I assume this was to create stakes, but since closing and reopening the game starts you off from just before you begin the mission, it's kind of pointless)

[strike]The much larger and more frustrating problem with the game is not the mechanics, however, but it's tendency to softlock largely at random, forcing you to close and reboot the game entirely.  I have played this game for 11 hours at the time of this review, and the game has softlocked no less than 5 times in that period.

There seem to be two recurring themes with the softlocks, and if the creators happen to see this review, maybe they can work on fixing them.  The softlocks I have repeatedly experienced are as follows

-When downloading from a data node, the game locks up during the step where it ticks down your download progress.  The game is not specifically frozen, but it hangs there without completing the download tick forever, preventing you from starting your turn or continuing.
-The exit command can sometimes completely cease to work, preventing you from leaving the mission either by inputting the command or hitting ESC (in essence, you get a message saying you are terminating the session, but nothing happens, no matter how many times you try, and the ESC key doesn't do anything) - this one is more insidious, as you don't often realize it's happened until you have completed the mission, and you are ready to leave, only to find that you have been softlocked for an unknown amount of time, thus wasting the entire effort you spent on the mission.

Assuming these two issues and any others I haven't found yet can be fixed, this is a great game.  But tonight won't be the first time since I started playing that I closed the game in frustration and went off to do something else after another softlock incident.[/strike]

Looks like this has been patched. :)

review_text_raw:
Its gameplay doesn't have much to do with real-life hacking but it will make you feel like a hacker.
It's a collection of tactical minigames in which you move through abstract networks avoiding or eliminating obstacles and collecting resources. That's basically it. Comparing Midnight Protocol to Hacknet doesn't make much sense because the games are so different mechanically.

In addition to solid tactical puzzles that get more complex as the game progresses, there's a strong narrative wtih rpg elements - you choose to be a good or a bad guy and the story adapts. It would take at least 2 playthroughs to see all the content (one playtrough took me 21 hrs including all side missions in turn-based mode). Visuals are top notch, minimalistic and elegant. (However, I miss the ability to rotate the view like in Invisible Inc.). Soundtrack is beautiful and atmospheric and great to listen to on its own (though main theme is a bit too melancholic for this type of game). Level design is really solid and customizable loadout makes it fun to experiment with different approaches. My favourite level is Monarch&Reiter because it's multistage, complex and non-linear.

Make sure to try out real-time mode as it changes the gameplay completely, making it more exciting and similar to real-life hacking (and much less RNG reliant). It's ideal for a second playthrough once you're familiar with the commands and stuff. 

I'd recommend it to all tactical turn-based and hacking games fans and to keyboard ninjas. I really like the game setup and would love to see a sequel with improvements primarily in the story department - the game has huge potential.

What an awesome game. As an avid Android:Netrunner player, I really enjoyed how the theme and story fit really together with the mechanics to create a great experience.

The game at it's core is split into two sides.
- the "prep" side where you chat with your contacts, choose what missions you'll accept, and what programs you'll bring.
- the "mission" side, which is an action-economy boardgame where you traverse a network of nodes towards an objective, break / avoid ICE, all while a trace timer counts up to your doom.

With such a solid core system, I would have expected any other developer to just "phone in" the actual level design, and just procedurally generate the missions, but this is not the case here. Instead, every mission is hand crafted, unique in it's own way, and you can really feel the attention to detail and love that was put into each experience, which is just so refreshing in the current state of gaming that ask you to just to the same thing over and over with minor variations.

[b]On RNG[/b]
Much of the criticism I see in other reviews talks about the "RNG" of tracing and ICE placements, but I have to disagree. Choosing between putting more of your resources into delaying the trace to play it slow and steady versus making the calculated mad dash to the finish is PEAK NETRUNNER. I will say that I started out playing very cautiously, and managing cloak slices while waiting for dagger to break through felt tedious. By the end, I had freed myself from my safe shell and embraced the run, preferring to sidestep, bypass, or just facetank ICE instead.

[b]On Playstyle[/b]
On a similar note, I do think that this game heavily encourages you to use different programs due to adapt to different the missions, so if you're a stickler for your favourite deck setup, you may find like you're trying to brute force your square solution into the circular hole. There's a bit of information revealed before you start a mission, letting you know if you should even bring a specific type of program. From there, you bring your favourite set and hope for the best. 

Should you fail, the game lets you quickly restart, or even backout to the pre-mission deck configuration step. A few of the other reviews find a way to complain about this, stating that "the game expects you to just lose on your first run, so that you can back out and come back in with perfect 'meta' knowledge", but again I disagree. 
- The initial run is thrilling, in a "discovering the unknown and doing my best with what I've got" way, which again, is PEAK NETRUNNER. I completed most missions with my initial deck configuration.
- The follow up / reconfigured / "meta informed" runs are also satisfying, in a "I am the ultimate runner, witness how I effortlessly defeat your defences" way. I found I preferred to swap to more "informed" setups after failing some of the harder story missions.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
I really recommend this game. It's fun, the mechanics and theme work great together, and the missions are all lovingly crafted and unique. I found myself saying "wow this is so cool" constantly.

I'm glad I stuck with this game long enough to get through my "safe shell" phase of tediously chipping away at ICE and managing cloak slices. While everyone starts out playing safe, it's nice when new programs become available to let you run a little more recklessly.

Always be running. [url=https://alwaysberunning.net/profile/645]-Lopert[/url]

I don't have many games in my library - I'm quite picky in my tastes. I'm not usually one for hacking games but the Demo left me wanting more. After 22 enjoyable hours, I'm evidently happy to have added this game in my library. I waited to give this revieuw untill I finished the story for the first time - It will certainly not be the last. I'll take some time to revieuw a few aspects of the game that might interest you most:

Gameplay/Mechanics: 8/10
A game is nothing without gameplay, and a hacking game sets a promise: it will not be just 'a game' - but one with depth, complexity, and decision making. To achieve this, Midnight protocol structures its gameplay around levels that feel like a labyrinth or puzzle. A Digital dungeon, if you will. To get around the various obstacles such as firewalls, encrypted nodes and 'antagonistic' system operators that chase you down you get access to hardware you can tailor to your playstyle, as well as a host of programs each with their own up- and downsides. You quickly learn how to balance them carefully, using fairly easy commands to allocate memory to the programs you need in order to finish the level. Suffice to say, Midnight protocol nails the hacker-feel you'll expect. It is not all roses and sunshine of course - there is quite a reliance on RNG to many of the mechanics of the game that can make you second guess your decisions while they are actually fine, or save you when you know you had no right to make it. Aside from that, i found myself at times trying a level, finding where the hidden obstacles were, and avoiding them alltogether once I got to reload the level. This was- at times-unavoidable, and felt wrong. I've since noticed that these hidden obstacles are slightly randomized, at least in some levels, which alleviated this somewhat. Perhaps the developers could not just list potential ICE, but also include a map at the beginning of the mission (once you enter a mission you see the layout anyway, except in rare instances), that does not show the obstacles, but layout of the nodes beforehand. With this information I feel I personally would not have had to reload to adapt my strategy as much as I did.

Story 9/10
An RPG without a story is not really an RPG at all, now is it?
The game starts you off as a hacker released after a while in custody. You reunite with a few old friends who help you get back into the swing of things, and in doing so, ease you into the virtual world.
I have to admit I struggled a little bit accepting this game as an RPG at first. Sure there was a fairly engaging story, but I didn't feel I had much say in it. This luckily changed a while after passing the tutorial missions.
The story was believable and fun for a while, Untill a brilliant twist that immediately reframed all my desisions I had made beforehand. And this is the reason I very much want to play again, making diffrent choices alltogether. This is even before the positively thrilling 'endgame ' that kept me up for hours after I should really have just gone to bed (They really made that 'hacker-in-a-dark-room thing work). I needed to KNOW - needed to SEE - and most importantly, I had a mission to complete. In short, the the story might feel sparse in the beginning, but it slowly builds into a memorable and spectacular experience I am glad to have had.

User Interface 6.5/10
Yes, i couldn't pick a 6 or a 7. I spent quite a while debating what score to give the UI. 
at first, it is a little jarring. not unreadable or inaccessible at all, but it CAN be hard to navigate. outside of missions. In addition, it can be easy to lose track of things if you've stopped playing for a moment and come back. This of course comes in part down to the decision to do away with a cursor and tie everything to the keyboard. Regardless of my grievances, I do not thing they should have gone for any other input - it is part of the charm and feeling.The game does give you the ability to move things around for the gamepay in-levels, for which i personall found little need to do but is a nice touch. If the 'mails' could be ordered somehow, like how i can do i nan actual mailbox i would very quickyl change the score, but as someoen who tried making games themselves i can see how this would be a huge time- and-money sink for relatively little gain. The UI is defenitely functional as is, and just takes a slight bit of getting used to.

With this said, the revieuw is already quite lengthy, and i think i did touch on the most important points. In summary, this game is very much worth it's full price - That's probably selling it short. I'm glad I didn't have to pay more - but I would have.

Midnight protocol is a brilliant game.

The hacking is presented through awesome animations and graphics. The game would've been completely different without them. The enemies, the programs, the firewalls. All of them have their own models and animations. The graphics is one of the pillars that sets Midnight Protocol apart from others.

The mechanics themselves are solid - you presented with a myriad of ways to create your own playstyle. Full stealth, full damage, bypass and damage, randomness, certainty. There are so many viable combinations that everyone will find something that fits them. Ah, and also, you interact with the game only through keyboard, which adds to the atmosphere.

The plot is cool by itself, and I will eat my keyboard if you are able to predict all the twists.

The final piece - the music. It is wonderful. I go to sleep with one of the themes playing in my head.
The music sets the atmosphere for different situations. 
Are you okay or about to be caught? Are you in the menu or in the battle? Is that a boss battle? There are not many tracks, but all of them are awesome.

Even in its full price, the game is worth it.
It's a unique experience.

review_text_raw:
I don't write reviews very often but this game deserves one.   Midnight Protocol is an accessible hacker game where it really makes you feel like you are hacking without having to have all the technical know-how.    You input commands into a terminal (via keyboard, how novel!) but there are not so many as to feel overwhelming.  In fact a few basic commands are designed to make it as transparent as possible (such as 'deck' which will remind you what you have equipped).  Some programs also have options and a simple 'help' command will remind you how to input them.  The game really hits the sweetspot with accessibility and it also has nice ambiance and interesting story line.    

I enjoyed the variety of programs and deck hardware to choose from though i found some quite powerful, some quite situational, and some unnecessary but there is a lot of fun in figuring that out for yourself.   While early on i used the standard 'cloak' and 'dagger' everyone starts with, i evolved my strategy to use 'mask' which is powerful but slow but wound up enjoying using 'onion' the most.   Combine that with the hardware that gives a modest stealth boost and see what happens!   Takes some discipline though.

I also randomly and luckily equipped 'Ace' and 'King' in the hack where it is needed the most.  It made the hack a breeze but I couldn't think of needing these programs in any other hack.  As I said, quite situational.  But the game is quite forgiving and as long as you have a program or piece of hardware in your inventory, you can easily rollback the hack and re-equip what you need to start that hack over.  
The rollback feature may make the game even a little too easy but with that said, i found the game engaging and rare for me, something i concentrated on completing before i got distracted by my next game!   My main criticism of the game may be that, while i don't want to go into detail and spoil it, there were components of the plot i didn't like.  Let's just say it was controversial.   But overall the meaningful side quests and decisions that you make but come back to help or haunt you help make the overall experience quite fun.

I would highly recommend this to anyone interested in the hacking universe and good story telling (all revealed via email).  As I write this i even have to remember i have a mouse I can use and don't have to only use the keyboard!  Enjoy!

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol, developed by LuGus Studios and published by Iceberg Interactive, is a masterfully constructed cyberpunk hacking RPG that forgoes the flashy aesthetics of most games in its genre in favor of tension, intellect, and immersion. It tells the story of a hacker known as Data, who is drawn back into the digital underworld after being doxxed and exposed. The narrative unfolds through encrypted emails, terse chat messages, and system logs, building a world of espionage, distrust, and digital warfare without ever showing a single human face. The game’s story is deeply personal, portraying the isolation and moral grayness of living behind the screen, where every keystroke carries risk and consequence. What begins as a simple act of self-defense quickly evolves into a web of political intrigue, corporate corruption, and cyber rebellion, all told through the restrained, text-based aesthetic of a command-line interface.

The most striking element of Midnight Protocol is its complete commitment to its design philosophy. Every action is performed through the keyboard—no mouse, no icons, just commands typed into a digital terminal. This approach is not merely a stylistic choice but a fundamental part of the experience. It places the player directly in the mindset of a hacker, forcing you to think in terms of efficiency, logic, and spatial reasoning. Networks are depicted as interconnected nodes, each representing firewalls, data caches, security systems, or hidden traps. Your goal varies from mission to mission: infiltrate corporate systems, extract sensitive data, disable rival programs, or manipulate information to your advantage. Each network functions as a puzzle, requiring you to manage limited resources, stay ahead of traces, and decide how far you can push before the system locks you out. Every move carries tension, and the thrill of narrowly escaping detection provides a constant pulse of adrenaline.

What makes these mechanics so engrossing is how they combine strategic planning with improvisation. Each mission feels like a high-stakes chess match played against invisible opponents. You have a library of programs at your disposal—some for stealth, others for brute-force attacks—and choosing the right combination is crucial. The trace system, which measures how close the authorities are to locating you, ensures that every decision feels urgent. Some players might find the reliance on randomness in the trace and detection mechanics slightly frustrating, as even well-planned strategies can fall apart under bad luck. Yet, this unpredictability mirrors the nature of hacking itself—controlled chaos within an unstable system. As your reputation grows and your alignment shifts between white-hat idealism, gray-hat pragmatism, and black-hat ruthlessness, the missions, tools, and story outcomes evolve to reflect your choices. This morality system adds replayability and depth, as it allows players to craft a hacker identity that aligns with their philosophy.

The game’s progression system is intricately tied to its tone of calculated mastery. Through black markets and secret contacts, you acquire new software, upgrade existing tools, and refine your build into a precise digital arsenal. Different playstyles emerge naturally—one player may rely on stealth programs to bypass ICE unnoticed, while another might embrace aggressive, virus-based attacks to dismantle defenses entirely. The learning curve is smooth but demanding, gradually pushing players toward mastery without resorting to handholding. It’s the kind of game that rewards patience and experimentation; every failure is a lesson in systems thinking. The world expands organically through your own initiative: new missions arrive via encrypted emails, hidden coordinates, or anonymous requests. Even the mundane act of checking your in-game inbox feels immersive, as if you are living within a network of digital conspiracies.

Visually, Midnight Protocol is minimalist yet elegant. The interface is clean, the color palette subdued but purposeful—shades of neon blue, black, and red evoke the cold pulse of cyberspace. Despite its simplicity, the design feels immersive, capturing the essence of a digital battlefield through pure abstraction. Every flicker of light and distortion effect contributes to the illusion that you are operating from the edge of legality. The sound design amplifies this immersion with sharp beeps, data pulses, and the low hum of electronic machinery that underscore each command you enter. There is no voice acting or cinematic interlude, but this absence enhances the sense of isolation and authenticity. You are a ghost in the network, unseen and unheard, communicating only through code and action.

The pacing of Midnight Protocol is deliberate, structured around cycles of tension and relief. Missions can be completed in short bursts, yet each one feels meaningful. There are no filler objectives; everything you do contributes to the unraveling of the narrative or your personal evolution as a hacker. While the game never overstays its welcome, some players may wish for a broader scope or more diverse mission environments. The story’s intimate scale, however, fits the tone—this is not about saving the world but about surviving it, carving your path through the static and deceit of a system that’s stacked against you. The writing is terse and precise, and though the characters are only ever seen through text, they feel real, shaped by ideology and consequence rather than cliché.

Midnight Protocol succeeds because it understands exactly what it wants to be—a cerebral, atmospheric strategy game that thrives on immersion, tension, and mechanical purity. It captures the loneliness and allure of the digital frontier, where information is power and morality is fluid. Its stripped-down design and keyboard-driven gameplay make it a niche experience, but within that niche lies something exceptional: a game that makes you feel like a real hacker, navigating systems not through spectacle, but through intellect. It’s a rare experience that balances narrative intrigue with strategic complexity, one that demands attention and rewards mastery. For those who crave precision, immersion, and the thrill of the unknown, Midnight Protocol is a digital labyrinth worth exploring line by line, command by command.

Rating: 8/10
